title: Foreign Investors Just Poured a Record $3.4 Billion Into Indian Government Bonds — and a Bloomberg Index Entry Could Unlock Billions More
excerpt: India's decision to scrap taxes on foreign bond investments, combined with falling oil prices and RBI reforms, has triggered the biggest monthly debt inflow on record and put Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index inclusion within reach
body:
A tectonic shift is under way in India's bond market, and it is happening faster than almost anyone expected.

Foreign investors bought a record ₹29,900 crore ($3.16 billion) of Indian government bonds through the Fully Accessible Route in June — more than double the $1.6 billion purchased in the entire January-to-May period combined. And the momentum has not slowed: in just the first two days of July, overseas buyers snapped up another $500 million, pushing total inflows since early June past $3.4 billion.

The catalyst was a sweeping set of reforms announced by New Delhi and the Reserve Bank of India on June 5. In a single stroke, India exempted foreign investors from the 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains tax on government bonds, scrapped the 20 per cent withholding tax on bond interest income, and broadened the pool of securities available under the Fully Accessible Route to include longer-dated sovereign debt.

"We believe that these changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt and systematic fixed income at State Street Investment Management, which manages roughly $5.6 trillion in assets.

## The Bloomberg Index Question

The real prize, however, may still be ahead. Market participants now widely expect Bloomberg Index Services to announce, potentially this month, whether Indian government bonds will be added to its flagship Global Aggregate Bond Index — one of the most widely tracked fixed-income benchmarks in the world.

India already entered the JPMorgan Government Bond Index-Emerging Markets last year. A Bloomberg inclusion would open the door to a second, even larger wave of passive foreign capital. Goldman Sachs projects that foreign flows into Indian government bonds could rise by $10 billion in 2026, in a note published this week.

"The removal of taxation on Indian government bonds will mechanically make them more interesting for global investors and will help redirecting flows towards the onshore market," said Niel Clement, a portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management.



> **""Unless the yield breaks below 6.75 per cent and closes there, we do not expect a sharp rally," a private bank trader told The Hindu BusinessLine."**


Shiv Chopra, a senior portfolio manager at BNP Paribas, added that India had now "aligned itself with other zero-tax sovereign issuers included in this index," removing one of the key structural barriers to inclusion.

## Yields Are Already Moving

The wall of money is showing up in bond prices. The benchmark 6.94 per cent 2036 bond yield has dropped to roughly 6.72 per cent — down 28 basis points over the past five weeks, its fifth straight weekly decline. Indian bonds gained even on Thursday, shrugging off a selloff in US Treasuries, as foreign appetite overwhelmed any residual caution.


![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)


The 10-year yield has hit a strong technical floor near 6.75 per cent, but traders said a Bloomberg inclusion announcement could push it decisively lower. "Unless the yield breaks below 6.75 per cent and closes there, we do not expect a sharp rally," a private bank trader told The Hindu BusinessLine. "But a formal index entry changes the calculus entirely."

Liquidity conditions have also improved, with the banking system swinging to a surplus of ₹1.12 lakh crore after a week of deficit — further easing pressure on borrowing costs.

## The Oil Backstop

The reforms arrived against an unusually favourable macro backdrop. Brent crude has retreated to roughly $70 per barrel, down from above $120 at the peak of the US-Iran conflict earlier this year. For oil-import-dependent India, every dollar off the price of a barrel directly improves the fiscal deficit, the current account and inflation expectations.

RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said at an event in Russia this week that India is unlikely to raise its official inflation target and that there may be a case for lowering it over the long term — a statement that further burnished India's appeal as a fixed-income destination.

The rupee, meanwhile, has logged its first quarter-on-quarter gain since March 2025, steadying around 95.27 per dollar. While analysts do not expect a dramatic appreciation, the removal of a key headwind — capital flight — is itself a stabiliser.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For diaspora Indians, the bond-market transformation has direct implications. The scrapping of capital gains and withholding taxes means that NRI investors can now hold Indian sovereign debt without the drag of double taxation that previously made it unattractive compared to US Treasuries or Singapore government bonds.

The RBI has also sweetened the deal for NRI deposits: it will bear hedging costs for non-resident foreign currency deposits of 3-to-5-year maturities raised by banks through September 30 — effectively offering a risk-free carry incentive.

With the 10-year Indian government bond yielding roughly 6.72 per cent (tax-free for foreign holders) versus the 10-year US Treasury at about 4.49 per cent, the spread has become one of the widest and most attractive in the emerging-market universe.

## The Road Ahead

India's bond market was, until recently, one of the most under-owned by foreign investors relative to its size. That is changing at pace. The combination of tax reform, index inclusion prospects, falling oil and a stabilising rupee has created what Goldman Sachs calls a "structural re-rating" of Indian fixed income.

For NRI investors who have traditionally favoured Indian equities, gold or real estate, the sovereign bond market has quietly become the most compelling opportunity in years. The question is no longer whether foreign money will flow in — it is how much, and how fast.
